concepts.title: Stack Size after Pushes and Pops

questions.q: Using the method 'Stack Size after Pushes and Pops', work with: pops = 4, pushes = 4, start_size = 2048. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of current_size.
questions.a: 2048 bytes

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Stack Size after Pushes and Pops' and work with: pops = 80, pushes = 6, start_size = 512. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of current_size.
questions.a: 438 bytes

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Stack Size after Pushes and Pops' refers to.
questions.a: A stack is a linear data structure that admits inserts and deletes at one end, the TOP, so it obeys LIFO: PUSH adds at the top, POP removes from the top, and the element stored last leaves first.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Stack Size after Pushes and Pops'.
questions.a: Popping the glass numbered 2 from the pile of Figure 3.2 exposes the glass beneath it, never a middle one.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Stack Size after Pushes and Pops', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: current_size = start_size + (pushes - pops)

concepts.title: Applications of the Stack in Practice

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Applications of the Stack in Practice' refers to.
questions.a: Everywhere the most recent item must be served first, a stack fits: reversing a string, undo and redo in editors, the BACK button of a browser replaying page history, and checking that parentheses in an expression nest correctly.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Applications of the Stack in Practice'.
questions.a: Browser history keeps visited pages as a stack, so two BACK clicks from page P3 land on page P1.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Applications of the Stack in Practice', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: most recent change -> undone or redone first

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Infix, Prefix and Postfix Notations' refers to.
questions.a: One expression has three written forms: infix places operators between operands as x * y + z, prefix (Polish) places them before the operands, and postfix (reverse Polish) places them after, which removes the need for parentheses and precedence rules.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Infix, Prefix and Postfix Notations'.
questions.a: Prefix and postfix expressions evaluate in one left-to-right traversal because operator order is already fixed.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Infix, Prefix and Postfix Notations', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: x * y + z -> +z*xy (prefix) -> xy*z+ (postfix)

questions.q: Using the method 'Evaluating a Postfix Expression', work with: the fixed constants of the method. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of result.
questions.a: 11 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Evaluating a Postfix Expression' and work with: the fixed constants of the method. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of result.
questions.a: 11 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Evaluating a Postfix Expression' refers to.
questions.a: A postfix expression evaluates with a stack: operands are pushed, and each operator pops two values, applies itself and pushes the result back, so the final single stack entry is the answer, as in 7 8 2 * 4 / + giving 11.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Evaluating a Postfix Expression'.
questions.a: Only operands are pushed during evaluation; each operator consumes exactly the top two stack values.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Evaluating a Postfix Expression', in plain ASCII form.

Evaluate A B + C * for A=3, B=5, C=1, showing the stack after each operation.. Use the method 'Postfix Evaluation with Letter Operands'. Work with: a_value = 20000, b_value = 80000, c_value = 12000. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of result.

Evaluate A B * C / D * for A=3, B=5, C=1, D=4.. Use the method 'Postfix Evaluation with Letter Operands'. Work with: a_value = 20000, b_value = 5000, c_value = 2500. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of result.
Explain in your own words what 'Postfix Evaluation with Letter Operands' refers to.
questions.a: When postfix operands are letters, substitute the given values first and then run the same push-pop evaluation, for example A B + C * with A=3, B=5, C=1 becomes (3 + 5) * 1 which is 8.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Postfix Evaluation with Letter Operands'.
questions.a: Substitute the letter values before evaluation so only numbers ride on the stack.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Postfix Evaluation with Letter Operands', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: result = (a_value + b_value) * c_value

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Converting Infix to Postfix' refers to.
questions.a: Algorithm 3.1 converts infix to postfix using a stack for operators: operands append straight to the output string, left parentheses wait on the stack, operators pop higher-precedence elders first, and a right parenthesis pops until its matching left one, discarding the pair.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Converting Infix to Postfix'.
questions.a: Only operators and parentheses ever ride on the stack during conversion; operands go directly to the output.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Converting Infix to Postfix', in plain ASCII form.
Explain in your own words what 'Matching Parentheses with a Stack' refers to.
questions.a: A compiler validates nesting by pushing every opening parenthesis and popping on every closing one; the expression is balanced only if each closing parenthesis finds its partner on the stack top and the stack ends empty.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Matching Parentheses with a Stack'.
questions.a: For ((2+3)*(4/2))+2 the two left parentheses are popped in reverse order, proving correct nesting.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Matching Parentheses with a Stack', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: balanced -> every ')' pops a '(' and final stack is empty

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Stack Implementation Using a List' refers to.
questions.a: Python builds a stack on a list whose right end is the TOP: append() plays PUSH, pop() plays POP, len() gives the size, and a helper checks emptiness so a pop from an empty stack reports underflow instead of crashing.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Stack Implementation Using a List'.
questions.a: Because append and pop act on the rightmost end, no explicit TOP variable is needed.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Stack Implementation Using a List', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: top element = stack_list[len - 1]
